# Chapter 1 (M0) — The yardstick: evaluation suite, verifier and data

*Milestone M0, 25–28 October 2026. Tables are generated by `scripts/report_m0_tables.py` from the
committed reports in `docs/reports/` and the suite file; decisions are in `docs/decisions/`.*

## 1.1 Purpose

The study asks whether RL post-training with verifiable rewards *sharpens* what a model already
solves (higher pass@1) or *expands* what it can solve (higher pass@k at large k). Both readings are
differences between evaluations of different checkpoints, so the evaluation itself must not move
between them. M0 fixes that yardstick before any training: the problem sets, the sampling and
scoring protocol, the verifier, the RL problem pool and its separation from every evaluation
problem. It also records the base model, Qwen3.5-4B-Base, on the frozen suite, which is the
reference every later checkpoint is compared with.

**Outcome.** Suite `soe-eval-v3` (suite file sha256 `533c2053…`): 2,452 problems in four levels plus
a 233-problem hard tier sampled at k = 64. The verifier accepts the equivalent notations the hand
audit found; it was checked against all 87,888 stored base-model samples with no false positive
found. The RL pool (RL train v3, 12,124 problems) is free of the reformatted and re-encoded copies
of evaluation problems that the original near-duplicate rule missed. The base reference is 50,416
samples. M0 used 304 GPU-hours, all on A40/A30/A10 except 0.1 h of A100 for container checks.

## 1.2 Evaluation suite

Four levels (decisions 002, 003):

- **Level A**, public benchmarks: MATH-500, AIME 2024, AIME 2025 and OlympiadBench (English,
  open-ended, text-only competition maths).
- **Level B**, in distribution: a split held out of the RL pool (DAPO-Math-17k) before any
  training, so that gains on it measure learning on the training distribution without training on
  the problems themselves.
- **Level C**, fresh and out of distribution: competitions after the base model's release (C1:
  AIME 2026, HMMT February 2026) and 2025 competitions absent from the RL pool (C2: BRUMO, CMIMC,
  HMMT February and November, SMT). Level C is never used for any selection.
- **Hard tier**: 250 problems from Levels A and B on which the base model is weak, sampled 64
  times so that pass@32 and pass@64 can show expansion (decision 005).

Base-model results per set, at the suite's main tier (16 samples per problem):

### Hard tier

The selection rule was registered before any selection sample existed (decision 005): a problem is
eligible if the base model solves at most 4 of 16 samples drawn with a *different* seed (seed 1)
from the evaluation seed (seed 0). Selecting on the evaluation seed would bias the subset towards
problems that were unlucky on that seed and regress upward afterwards: on the same 250 problems the
selection seed gave pass@1 0.048 and the independent evaluation seed 0.062 (BF16 v1 run). Of 524
eligible problems a stratified draw took 250 (OlympiadBench 110, Level B 113, MATH-500 13, AIME 2024
7, AIME 2025 7). The frozen file and its hash never changed; later findings removed problems from
the tier without refilling it (1.5): 9 have a wrong or ambiguous gold, and 8 met the rule only
because the verifier rejected correct answers. The tier in the v3 reference is 233 problems.

## 1.3 Protocol

The protocol follows Yue et al. (2025), with the same settings for every checkpoint: base, SFT,
DPO and every RL run.

| Setting | Value | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| temperature / top-p / top-k | 0.6 / 0.95 / -1 | 004 |
| max new tokens (also the RL rollout cap) | 16384 | 004, 006 |
| vLLM seed per request | 0 | 004 |
| KV cache | fp8 | 009 |
| chat template, thinking mode | True, True | 006 |
| answer | last \boxed{}; else last 2-3 final-answer boxes joined | 004, 010 |
| truncated response | incorrect | 004 |
| main tier k | 1, 4, 8, 16 | 004 |
| hard tier k | 1, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 | 005 |

Two settings were measured before being fixed:

- **Thinking mode** (decision 006). Qwen3.5's chat template opens a `<think>` block when thinking
  is on. On the format probe, accuracy with and without it differed by −1.0 ± 1.6 points, but about
  35% of base-model samples hit the 16K cap. The cap stays, because it is also the RL rollout cap.
  Truncated samples count as wrong.
- **FP8 KV cache** (decision 009, the user's choice). On an A40 it stores 1.69M tokens of KV cache
  against about 960K in BF16 (1.75×), for about 1.25× the sampling throughput. Calibrated scales
  are not available for this hybrid-attention model in vLLM 0.24, so keys and values use a scale of
  1.0. The effect on accuracy is measured in 1.8.

## 1.4 Data

The RL pool is DAPO-Math-17k (English, deduplicated). The build (decisions 003, 007, 011) removed
679 exact duplicates and 201 near-duplicates of evaluation or Level B problems, then carved out
Level B.

| File | v2 (decision 007) | v3 (decision 011) |
|---|---|---|
| rl/level_b (Level B; 983 after the suite's exclusions) | 994 | unchanged |
| rl/train (RL pool) | 12232 | 12124 |
| evaluation files | 11 sets, byte-identical to v1 | unchanged |

Two corrections followed the first build:

- **Text repair** (decision 007). 640 of 14,116 raw DAPO rows carried encoding debris; for example
  `\frac` was stored as a form feed followed by "rac". The repair was made in place, so Level B kept
  its 994 problem ids (42 repaired) and the train pool kept its split (585 repaired, 4 duplicates
  dropped). On the 42 repaired Level B problems the base model scored pass@1 0.897 on the damaged
  text and 0.872 on the repaired text, within seed noise. A full rebuild was rejected because it
  would have replaced 379 of the 994 Level B problems.
- **Copies of evaluation problems** (decision 011; 1.6).

## 1.5 Verifier and gold answers

The verifier extracts the last `\boxed{}` and compares it with the gold answer using math-verify.
Three checks shaped it.

**Hand audit** (M0.8). 200 base-model answers, drawn from 3,785 candidates by risk category, were
judged by hand. 107 correct verdicts and 53 incorrect verdicts were confirmed; 2 were left unsure;
38 answers judged wrong by the verifier were in fact correct. **No false positives were found.** The
false negatives were notation, not mathematics: a tuple for a column vector, percent signs, labels
(`w=16, d=3`), words between answers, ordinals, an inequality for an interval, two sets for a flat
list, a family of solutions written with n instead of k.

**Fixes** (decision 008). When math-verify rejects, both answers are rewritten to one notation and
compared again; a pair is accepted if either comparison accepts it, so the rewrites only add
acceptances. 30 of the 38 false negatives are now accepted. The remaining 8 are answers to
excluded problems, two gold strings that are format debris (excluded), and one equivalent family of
solutions written with period π/2, kept as a known rejection. Every case is a pinned unit test,
alongside guards that the rewrites keep wrong answers wrong. Re-judging all 87,888 stored samples
changed 703 verdicts, all from wrong to correct, from 83 distinct answers on 22 problems; every one
was checked by hand.

**Split answers** (decision 010). In 121 of the 50,416 v3 samples, on 24 OlympiadBench problems,
the model boxed the parts of a multi-part answer separately (`\boxed{64} and \boxed{1/4}`). When
the last box is wrong, the verifier now also tries the last two or three boxes of the final answer
(after `</think>`) joined with commas. Exactly those 121 samples changed: Level A pass@1 rose by
0.47 points. The same function is the RL reward. The report stage re-scores every stored
completion, so a verifier change reaches old samples without re-sampling.

**Gold screen.** A problem is flagged when at least 75% of its samples agree on one answer that the
verifier rejects. 25 problems were flagged: 10 had a wrong gold, 3 an ambiguous question, 9 were
verifier false negatives, 2 had a gold that was format debris, and 1 was the model's error.
Together with the audit this gives the suite's lists:

| List in the suite | Problems |
|---|---|
| excluded_problems (wrong, ambiguous or unreadable gold) | 21 |
| removed_from_hard_subset (verifier false negatives) | 8 |
| hard tier in the v3 report (frozen file of 250, minus both lists) | 233 |

Excluded problems stay in the frozen files but are never sampled or scored. Public benchmarks are
excluded, not re-written, so the remaining problems stay comparable with published numbers.

## 1.6 Contamination of the RL pool

The build dropped a training problem holding at least half of an evaluation or Level B problem's
word 13-grams. That rule leaves no residual overlap, but it misses copies: LaTeX formatting breaks
13-word runs (`$1/6$` against `\frac{1}{6}`), and DAPO re-encodes answers ("all pairs" becomes
"the sum of all elements"). A sensitivity analysis (`scripts/contamination_report.py`) listed 354
train/reference pairs sharing at least 20% of 13- or 8-grams and classified them. All 121 pairs
that are identical after formatting, reworded with the same data, or share the answer were read
by hand. 108 training problems were dropped because they are the same problem as a reference: 86
reformatted or reworded, 21 with the answer re-encoded, 1 being part (a) of a multi-part
reference. They had copied 74 Level B and 24 Level A problems. 12 were kept as genuine variants
(different data, a different question, or a match only on answer-format boilerplate). Variants
with different numbers were kept on purpose; they teach a technique on other data, as any training
data does.

| Check | RL train v2 | RL train v3 |
|---|---|---|
| residual at the frozen rule (13-grams >= 0.5) | 0 | 0 |
| option 1: identical_text (E) | 52 | 0 |
| option 2: same_problem (E, R, or same answer) | 120 | 12 |
| option 3: plus_close_variants (option 2, or share >= 0.3) | 187 | 79 |
| option 4: everything_listed (share >= 0.2) | 338 | 230 |

The SFT data does not exist yet. Its check against all three levels, with the same method, moved
to M2.

## 1.7 Base-model reference

Qwen3.5-4B-Base (revision `1001bb4d…`) on `soe-eval-v3`: 50,416 samples, scored at commit
`d72167c`.

| Level | Problems | pass@1 | pass@4 | pass@8 | pass@16 | maj@16 | truncated | mean tokens |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 1224 | 0.744 | 0.814 | 0.836 | 0.856 | 0.819 | 0.242 | 6225 |
| B | 983 | 0.672 | 0.807 | 0.844 | 0.872 | 0.809 | 0.306 | 8735 |
| C1 | 62 | 0.335 | 0.475 | 0.526 | 0.565 | 0.516 | 0.655 | 13394 |
| C2 | 183 | 0.385 | 0.510 | 0.548 | 0.585 | 0.508 | 0.598 | 12845 |

| Hard tier | Problems | pass@1 | pass@16 | pass@32 | pass@64 | maj@64 | truncated |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| all | 233 | 0.070 | 0.362 | 0.431 | 0.489 | 0.318 | 0.904 |
| A | 127 | 0.057 | 0.312 | 0.378 | 0.433 | 0.268 | 0.931 |
| B | 106 | 0.085 | 0.423 | 0.496 | 0.557 | 0.377 | 0.872 |

Three observations frame the later milestones:

- **The gap between pass@1 and pass@16 is wide on every level**, from 11 points on Level A to 23
  on Level C1. Sampling alone already solves many problems that a single attempt misses, which is
  the headroom both the sharpening and the expansion readings compete for.
- **Truncation dominates the hard tier.** 90% of its samples hit the 16K cap, and every sample that
  stopped on its own contains a boxed answer. On these problems the base model mostly runs out of
  length rather than giving a wrong answer, so changes in response length will matter as much as
  changes in correctness.
- **Level C is the hardest and the most truncated** (pass@1 0.34 and 0.39, 60–66% truncated) and
  has the fewest problems (62 and 183). Differences on it need wide error bars.

## 1.8 Protocol sensitivity

The FP8 decision was tested by re-sampling the whole base reference with FP8 and comparing it
problem by problem with the earlier BF16 reference. Both runs used the same scorer, before decision
010. Values are FP8 minus BF16, as a mean over problems ± paired standard error. The control row
compares two BF16 runs that differ only in seed, on Levels A and B.

| Comparison | Problems | pass@1 (points) | pass@k (points) |
|---|---|---|---|
| level A | 1224 | +0.35 ± 0.21 | +1.72 ± 0.51 (pass@16) |
| level B | 983 | +0.15 ± 0.32 | +0.20 ± 0.66 (pass@16) |
| level C1 | 62 | +0.60 ± 1.33 | +4.84 ± 3.58 (pass@16) |
| level C2 | 183 | +0.10 ± 0.74 | -4.92 ± 2.36 (pass@16) |
| hard tier | 233 | +0.11 ± 0.27 | +3.00 ± 2.23 (pass@64) |
| control: BF16 seed 1 − seed 0, level A | 1224 | +0.28 ± 0.20 | +1.06 ± 0.47 (pass@16) |
| control: BF16 seed 1 − seed 0, level B | 941 | +0.23 ± 0.34 | +0.53 ± 0.68 (pass@16) |

The FP8 shift on pass@1 is under one point everywhere and within seed noise. The Level A pass@16
difference has the same sign and a similar size as the BF16 seed control, so it comes from the BF16 seed-0
draw rather than from FP8. The Level C2 pass@16 drop (2 standard errors, 183 problems, one of ten
comparisons) is weak evidence and is not treated as an FP8 effect. All later comparisons use the v3
(FP8) reference.

0.94 worker-hours per shard of 96 on a mixed A40/A30/A10 pool.

## 1.10 Limitations and what moves on

- **Unchanged verdicts are checked by sampling, not exhaustively.** The audit read 200 answers.
  math-verify compares bare comma lists as sets, so an ordered answer given as a bare list could
  pass reordered; the audit found no case of it.
- **The gold screen cannot judge truncated problems.** It needs 75% agreement among all samples, so
  it is blind to most of the hard tier, where 90% of samples are truncated.
- **One known wrong gold remains.** Level B problem `dapo/254353b7…` has gold 2, which is
  impossible. It is excluded in a suite revision before the first SFT checkpoint is evaluated
  (plan, M2); it is one of 983 Level B problems.
- **The contamination review is one reader's judgement.** It covers pairs above 20% n-gram
  overlap. Pairs, verdicts and reasons are committed (`docs/reports/m0_train_v3_review.json`) so the
  review can be audited.
- **Moved out of M0.** The SFT-pool contamination check moves to M2. The development model and the
  assignment of GPU types to runs move to the G0 memo in M1. FASTER's A100s are 40 GB, which makes
  full-BF16 4B RL on two of them tight; M1 measures it.
